I’m using the PDF skill to read the bugbash sheet, the Discourse Graphs writing skill for the test cases, and the Turborepo skill for the combined build checks.

content.text:
Linear clarifies an important expectation: source edits sync to shared storage, but destination import and refresh are manual. Refresh is also allowed to overwrite local edits to an imported node. I’ll use that contract when judging the cases marked uncertain in the PDF.

The live project also has more regressions to recheck than the meeting notes list, including media embeds, duplicate titles, automatic Source import, and source-space naming. ENG-2297 is still in Backlog, so discovery with suggestive mode off remains an unresolved test case.

content.text:
I’m expanding the matrix along three dimensions: all four directions (R→R, R→O, O→R, O→O), different users and group memberships, and changes after the first import.

The most valuable combined-work case is three-space collaboration: A shares a node, B imports it and relates a new B-owned node to it, then A and C import B’s node. That checks origin identity, access to both endpoints, schema acceptance, and relation deduplication together. I’ll also include two users editing the same Roam source graph, since that exercises sync ownership and authorship in a way separate-vault tests don’t.

The matrix now has 100 scenarios, expanding to 346 direction-specific runs if we execute every applicable route. I’ll give it a smaller first-session order so the team can start with the highest-value combinations.

Two cases deserve early attention: equal source-local IDs in different spaces, because Obsidian discovery currently filters on that ID alone; and relation changes after import, because refreshing node content may not reconcile the surrounding relations. These are source-based risk findings, not live reproductions.

I’ve assembled the combined candidate and written **100 test scenarios**, with steps, expected results, applicable directions, and links to the existing work.

The main artifacts are:

- **[Full test matrix](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925/validation/roam-obsidian-2026-09-25/TEST-MATRIX.md)** — all 100 scenarios.
- **[Setup and session order](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925/validation/roam-obsidian-2026-09-25/README.md)** — people, groups, fixtures, and a practical sequence.
- **[Baseline and known gaps](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925/validation/roam-obsidian-2026-09-25/BASELINE.md)** — exact PR heads, integration decisions, and unresolved expectations.

**The combined build is ready for internal testing. Manual product validation has not been run yet.**

The candidate is at commit `09d97321` on `validation/roam-obsidian-20260925`, in [this dedicated worktree](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925).

It combines current main with:

| PR | Included work |
|---|---|
| [#1383](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1383) | Review and accept imported relation types and triples |
| [#1475](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1475) | Consistent schema metadata between sync and publish |
| [#1477](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1477) | Retry failed Roam asset copies |
| [#1479](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1479) | Roam import dialog and feedback |
| [#1482](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1482) | Obsidian import filenames |
| [#1412](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1412) | Round-trip tests, adapted to current main |

The five runtime merges were clean. The older round-trip test stack needed small harness updates and the current `[[@placeholder]]` expectation. The explicitly iceboxed post-v0 refactors are excluded; the baseline records the other exclusions.

Loadable, production-configured bundles are available here:

- **[Roam extension folder](/home/sid/Downloads/roam-obsidian-bugbash-20260925-09d97321/roam)**
- **[Obsidian plugin folder](/home/sid/Downloads/roam-obsidian-bugbash-20260925-09d97321/obsidian)**

Frozen install, all eight workspace type-check tasks, all six unit-test tasks, and both builds pass. That includes **600 Roam tests and 87 Obsidian tests**. The exported bundles are hash-verified.

The testing model needs **four directed paths: RR, RO, OR, OO**. RO and OR exercise different implementations. Alongside those, we need multiple users in one Roam graph and three distinct collaborating spaces.

One expectation from Linear matters throughout: **source edits sync to shared storage; destination refresh is manual, and refresh may overwrite edits to the imported copy**. Automatic destination updates and bidirectional text merging are outside v0. This resolves the uncertainty about polling in the older sheet. [Project scope](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/project/push-and-pull-nodes-between-roam-and-obsidian-49473d9eeb09)

The inventory covers:

| Area | Cases | What we exercise |
|---|---:|---|
| Sharing and access | 12 | First publish, multiple groups, outsiders, revoked/restored access, private dependencies, login changes, sharing/suggestive-mode combinations |
| Import, content, and identity | 12 | Markdown structure, filenames, duplicate titles, repeated imports, mixed batches, equal local IDs from different spaces |
| Updates and refresh | 12 | Source edits, local edits, rename, refresh-all partial failures, deletion/recreation, asset changes, Source/schema-only changes |
| Assets | 12 | Images/PDF/audio/video, paths, deduplication, same filename with different bytes, replacement, size limits, failures and retries |
| Source documents | 10 | Automatic Source import, reuse, missing/private Sources, placeholder repair, multiple Sources, changed references, returning to an original Source |
| Schemas and relations | 16 | Existing/new types, metadata consistency, templates, provisional schemas, instance acceptance, missing endpoints, deletion, direction, canvas use |
| Collaboration | 12 | Three-space relations, private endpoints, cycles, fan-out, multiple Roam editors, overlapping sync/import, authorship, cloned identities |
| Recovery and combined UX | 14 | Partial batches, relations failing after nodes succeed, interruption/restart, sorting/selection, result links, provenance, returning to normal work |

Expanding every applicable direction gives **346 individual executions**. That is the coverage inventory; the session guide groups them into workflows that reuse fixtures.

The most valuable combined-work scenario is this:

1. **A publishes node `a`.**
2. **B imports `a`, creates its own node `b`, relates `b` to imported `a`, and publishes `b`.**
3. **A imports `b` and should connect it to its original `a`.**
4. **C imports both and should see the correct tentative relation between those origins.**

Then repeat with C lacking access to `a`, with renamed endpoints, and after acceptance and refresh. This simultaneously exercises origin identity, group access, endpoint mapping, schema acceptance, and deduplication. The matrix includes all eight three-space platform combinations.

A second essential workflow uses **two people in the same Roam source graph**: A publishes, B edits the body or adds an asset, and either client performs the sync. We need to verify freshness, retry behavior, and authorship together.

There are already several specific places to probe:

- **ENG-2297 remains unresolved.** The candidate still gates Roam import discovery on suggestive mode. This is a known gap to record separately from subsequent import tests.
- **Obsidian discovery may conflate equal local IDs from different spaces.** Discovery filters on the local ID alone, while materialization uses fuller identity. This is a source-based risk, not a live reproduction.
- **Node refresh does not establish relation reconciliation.** Upstream relation deletion, retargeting, and preservation of local acceptance need explicit testing and a clear expected policy.
- **Asset recovery differs by failure location.** Sync failures can retry automatically; publish failures require republishing; assets reached only through another page’s embed have an accepted retry limitation.
- **Source-only and schema-only changes need their own cases.** Timestamp-based skipping can make these behave differently from editing the Evidence body.

I’d start with the four basic publish/import/refresh paths, then Source and media regressions, relation acceptance, the three-space workflow, and the shared-Roam-user/access cases. Those combinations should expose the most consequential gaps between the separately completed features.

lets discuss this first, the logistics

 A good idea can be if we make a pr for it and then for a bunch of grouped tests you make one testing video and we attach to the pr wdyt??? what are other better ways to do this??

**Yes, a draft validation PR with one video per group of tests is a good fit here.** It gives us a concrete combined build, CI results, and one place for the team to inspect the work.

I’d add a small test-results table alongside the videos. The videos show what happened; the table makes coverage, failures, and remaining work easy to see.

The setup I’d use is:

1. **One draft integration PR for the combined candidate.** Its description names the included PRs and links to the test plan and loadable builds. We explicitly mark it as a validation branch, since its diff contains work already being reviewed in other PRs.
2. **Group tests around complete user workflows.** For example, publish → import → edit → refresh; Evidence with Sources and assets; or three-space collaboration with relations. Each recording follows a coherent workflow and identifies the cases it covers.
3. **One result entry per group and candidate version.** Record the commit, directions tested, pass/fail/blocked cases, video, and linked bugs.
4. **Fixes go into focused PRs.** We incorporate them into the combined candidate, rerun the affected group, and run a small cross-product smoke check.

The important detail is **pinning each recording to the build it tested**. Once we add another fix, an earlier video remains evidence for the earlier candidate. We should be able to tell which results still apply and which need a rerun.

For recording logistics, I’d capture the testing session as we execute it, then attach a short walkthrough of each completed group with timestamps or case IDs. That preserves useful failure evidence while giving reviewers something manageable to watch. A group with failures still gets a recording and an honest result.

There are three reasonable places to organize this:

| Approach | Strength | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| **Draft PR as the main home** | Code, build, CI, discussion, and videos are together | The combined diff can be noisy; the PR changes as its constituent PRs merge |
| **Linear validation ticket as the main home** | Stable place for progress, blockers, bugs, and the release decision | Needs links back to the exact candidate build |
| **Shared test sheet as the main home** | Easiest for several developers to record results simultaneously | Needs disciplined links to commits, evidence, and issues |

**My preference is a light hybrid: the draft PR holds the candidate and videos; the existing internal-validation ticket holds the overall outcome and blocking bugs.** We keep one authoritative results table and link to it from both.

For our first few videos, I’d group them like this:

- **Basic lifecycle:** all four directions, repeated import, upstream edits, refresh, and rename.
- **Sources and assets:** available/missing Source, placeholder repair, media, deduplication, and retry.
- **Relations and collaboration:** schema acceptance, instance acceptance, canvas use, and A → B → C.
- **Access and recovery:** private dependencies, revoked access, partial failure, and multiple users in one Roam graph.

That gives us a reviewable record of the combined product, with a clear route from a failed test to its fix and retest.

I'd keep the core of your idea (everyone tests one shared head, with visual proof) but change three things.

1. Put the evidence on Linear, not a PR from the integration branch.
- That PR's diff would be about 2k lines, the sum of five open PRs that were already reviewed one by one.
- Two of those PRs are still changing: ENG-2131 has changes requested and ENG-2296 is a draft.
- It can never merge, and every rebase of one of those PRs makes the videos out of date.

We already have the right home. ENG-1883 is "Run internal MVP0 validation and capture follow-up issues", and the test matrix fits ENG-1881, "Document manual internal QA script for MVP0". Results, videos, and one ticket per failure can live there, and they'll outlast the PRs. If you want one SHA everyone builds from, push the branch without opening a PR. pnpm ci:validate already passes on it locally.

2. Record user journeys, not test groups, and make each recording a test.
The video tooling can check results inside the recording, and it can show Roam and Obsidian side by side. So instead of about 15 groups × 4 directions, I'd do about 6 recordings:
- one per direction (RR, RO, OR, OO), each covering share → discover → import → edit at source → refresh → accept relation
- the three-space relation case from your sheet
- a round trip, Roam → Obsidian → Roam

Each recording then passes or fails on its checks, so you can re-run it after ENG-2131 or ENG-2296 changes. What it needs:
- It only runs against local Supabase.
- RR needs Playwright slot 2 logged back in, since the dev graph is read-only.
- Access tests need a second account that isn't in the group.
- Per your rule, recording happens in a separate session.

There are a few parts of the other proposal I’d refine.

**Separate how we test from how we record evidence.** “CI, recording, or manual” mixes two different decisions. A manually discovered failure can later become an automated regression test and have a video.

I’d give each case two fields:

| Field | Options |
|---|---|
| Execution method | Automated conversion/contract test; local database test; real-product bugbash |
| Evidence | Assertion output/log; screenshot; failure video |

That also keeps us honest about coverage. Converter tests can establish title conversion or Source mapping. They don’t establish that publishing, authentication, storage, and the actual destination importer work together. We still need a complete user journey in each of RR, RO, OR, and OO.

**Don’t wait to establish the underlying cause before preserving a failure.** During testing, capture the steps, actual result, identities, logs, and relevant fixture state immediately. Then reproduce it and record in the separate recording session. We can consolidate several failures into one video once we know they share a cause. Similar-looking failures across Roam and Obsidian could have different causes.

**The same reproduction should support the fix.** This is the strongest part of the proposal: establish an expected result, show the candidate violating it, then rerun that same check against the fix. Where practical, turn the reproduction into a regression test. The video makes the failure understandable; the check keeps detecting it later.

**Passing cases need a small receipt, not necessarily a video.** I’d record the case and direction, candidate commit, environment, tester, and observed result. For example, “refresh updated the existing page UID and retained one Source relation” is more useful than just “passed.” Add a screenshot when the result is visual.

**Keep product questions distinct from bugs.** Upstream relation deletion is a good example: before calling the result wrong, we need to decide what should happen to an imported relation that somebody has accepted locally. Code reading can mark this as a high-risk case or a decision needed; it shouldn’t predetermine a failure.

One other detail: we should define “Roam → Obsidian → Roam round trip” carefully. An adapter round trip is valuable. For a user journey, the meaningful return flow is often **A shares a node; B imports it, creates a new B-owned node referring to it, and A imports B’s contribution**. Simply republishing an imported copy could exercise behavior we intentionally don’t support.

- **Bug tickets:** minimal reproductions and failure videos.
- **Focused fix PRs:** regression checks and the corresponding passing reproduction.

I’d divide the work like this:

| Responsibility | This session | Other session |
|---|---|---|
| Combined candidate | Own the branch, build configuration, artifacts, and candidate updates | Check that the included work and exclusions are correct |
| Test coverage | Maintain the canonical matrix and assign cases | Challenge it: missing scenarios, incorrect expectations, weak assertions |
| Execution | Drive complete journeys through the real apps | Run targeted automated/database checks and investigate suspected gaps |
| Findings | Consolidate results, duplicates, and release blockers | Supply reproducible findings and independently check important failures |
| Videos | Coordinate a later recording session for selected failures | Supply the minimal reproduction and expected result |

That gives us useful parallelism now: while one session establishes what actually happens, the other looks for what we forgot to ask.

A few coordination rules would make this work:

1. **Freeze one candidate and specify its environment.**  
   Use one commit, recorded builds, backend, database/migration version, feature settings, and account memberships. Matching source code is insufficient if one session uses local Supabase and the other uses the deployed backend. The environment needs to be explicit before either reports a result.

2. **Give every shared artifact one writer.**  
   This session owns the integration branch and canonical results. The other works in its own worktree and contributes findings or test commits. We each write our own result files, then consolidate them. This also follows the existing worktree ownership convention.

3. **Treat browser sessions, vaults, and test data as shared resources.**  
   Initially, one session controls the live apps while the other runs independent checks. Parallel live testing becomes useful once we have separate profiles, vaults, fixtures, and compatible backend setup. Neither session should reload the other’s extension or reset a database the other is using.

4. **Exchange evidence with each finding.**  
   A useful handoff contains: case and direction, candidate/environment, fixture, action, expected result, actual result, and evidence. Label it **suspected from code**, **reproduced**, or **needs a product decision**. That prevents a plausible code concern from becoming a “confirmed bug” through repetition.

5. **Keep failure discovery separate from fixing and recording.**  
   Preserve the reproduction first. Give each fix one owner and its own branch. Integrate fixes at a checkpoint, then rerun affected cases and the short smoke journeys. Record the failures that benefit from visual explanation in the separate recording session we discussed.

For communication, I’d use a small shared handoff directory with one file owned by each session. Both can read it; neither overwrites the other’s findings.
